title: Persuasion: Ethos, Pathos and Logos
summary: Aristotle named three ways a speech persuades: the speaker's character, the listeners' feelings, and the argument itself. Here's what he meant, and how debaters use all three truthfully.

p: In the *Rhetoric*, written in the 300s B.C., Aristotle defined rhetoric as the ability to see, in any case, "the available means of persuasion." He divided the means that come from the speech itself into three kinds:

rows: **Ēthos** (character)
"The personal character of the speaker": the audience believes a speaker who seems trustworthy.
Being fair to the other side, accurate with evidence, prepared, and calm.
**Pathos** (feeling)
"Putting the audience into a certain frame of mind": emotions change how people judge.
Showing the real people affected by an impact, so the judge feels why it matters.
**Logos** (argument)
"The proof, or apparent proof, provided by the words of the speech itself."
Claims, warrants, evidence and weighing.
table.note: Quotations from the W. Rhys Roberts translation.

sections.h: Ethos: character shown in the speech
p: Aristotle meant the character a speaker shows *through the speech*, not their reputation before it. In Book II he says listeners trust a speaker who shows good sense (practical wisdom), good character, and good will toward the audience. A debater shows these by knowing the topic, being honest about evidence, treating the opponent fairly, and speaking to the judge with respect. That's one more reason to [steelman](/debate/learn/steelman-vs-strawman/): fairness is persuasive.

Aristotle studied the emotions closely (anger, fear, pity, confidence and more) because people judge differently when they feel differently. Emotion is a fair tool when it shows the true weight of a real impact. It becomes unfair when it replaces evidence, as in an [appeal to pity](/logic/informal-logic/appeal-to-pity/) or language chosen only to inflame (see [Emotive and Loaded Language](/logic/informal-logic/loaded-language/)).
A good test: if you took away the emotional words, would the argument still stand? If yes, the feeling is helping the judge understand. If no, it's covering a gap.

For Aristotle, the core of persuasion is argument. He named two forms used in speeches: the **enthymeme**, a deductive argument that starts from what the audience already accepts and often leaves a step unstated, and the **example**, an argument from a similar case. Debaters use both every round: "Like the last time the state tried this..." is an argument from example; "Students need sleep, and early start times cut sleep, so..." is an enthymeme.
Aristotle also sorted speeches by their audience and purpose. Debate formats map onto them neatly.

rows: **Deliberative** (political)
The future
Is this course of action helpful or harmful?
Policy, Public Forum, Congress, parliamentary motions
**Judicial** (forensic)
The past
Was this act just or unjust?
Mock trial; fact resolutions about what happened
**Epideictic** (ceremonial)
The present
Is this honorable or shameful, worthy of praise or blame?
Speeches of tribute; value arguments about what deserves respect

list: **"Ethos means credentials."** Credentials help, but Aristotle's ethos is the character shown by the speech itself.
**"Pathos is manipulation."** Aristotle treats emotion as a legitimate part of judgment. Manipulation is emotion used without truth behind it.
**"The three are equal parts of a triangle."** Modern textbooks draw a "rhetorical triangle," but Aristotle gave argument the central place and treated the other two as supporting it.

example.title: One impact, three ways (Resolution: Communities should fund more public libraries)

lines.s: Libraries give free internet access; many families without home internet depend on them for school and job applications.
Picture a student finishing homework in a library because there's no internet at home, until the branch closes early.
The other side is right that budgets are tight, and we don't propose new buildings. We propose longer hours at the branches we have.

example.note: The strongest speeches use all three: a clear argument, a real person the judge can picture, and a fair-minded speaker the judge trusts.

practice: Take a contention from a topic page and add one sentence of pathos and one sentence of ethos without changing the logic.
Read Lincoln's Gettysburg Address (Harvard Classics, February 12) and mark one example of each mode.
Find an advertisement that relies on pathos alone. What argument (logos) is missing?
